title: COVID-19 Information on YouTube: Analysis of Quality and Reliability of Videos in Eleven Widely Spoken Languages across Africa
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 562 COVID-19 YouTube videos in eleven languages widely spoken across Africa. Each video was classified by two language-proficient medical raters into one of four mutually exclusive content types, one of which is 'misleading (scientifically inaccurate information or content that is not evidence-based)'; the paper reports 12/562 (2.13%) misleading. That is a share of items judged for accuracy against an external standard (WHO/CDC-derived criteria), so it meets the CONTENT criterion. The MICI and DISCERN instruments are additionally reported as scale means and are entered as QUALITY rows, excluded from prevalence.

estimates.country: Not specified; videos were sampled by language, in eleven languages widely spoken or representative of all regions of Africa (English, isiZulu, isiXhosa, Afrikaans, Nigerian Pidgin, Hausa, Twi, Arabic, Amharic, French, Swahili). No country filter was applied to the search
estimates.measure_type: % of COVID-19 YouTube videos classified as misleading
estimates.denominator: 562 YouTube videos containing COVID-19 medical or epidemiological information: for each of eleven languages the first 50 relevant results were screened for each of the search terms 'coronavirus' and 'COVID-19' plus the language name (75 videos for English), after excluding non-medical, wrong-language, no-audio and duplicate videos
estimates.definition: A video counted in the numerator if two independent language-proficient medical raters assigned it the content type 'misleading', defined as scientifically inaccurate information or content that is not evidence-based; the four content types (informative, misleading, personal, news update) are mutually exclusive, so a personal-experience or news video containing inaccurate claims would not be counted here
estimates.misinfo_def: "The type of content was classified into four distinct groups: informative (factual information regarding prevention, screening, signs, and symptoms, testing, treatment, and epidemiology), misleading (scientifically inaccurate information or content that is not evidence-based), personal (based on an individual's experience or that of a friend or family), and news updates"
estimates.source_quote: The majority of videos were classified as informative (471/562, 83.8%) with over 229 million views, while misleading videos constituted 12/562 (2.13%) of total videos, with a total number of views at over 75,000.
estimates.page_loc: Results 3.1 (Viewer Interaction Metrics); also Abstract ('Informative videos (471/562, 83.8%) accounted for the majority, whilst misleading videos (12/562, 2.13%) were minimal') and Table 2 (Content rows) / Table 3 (per-language)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Videos in each language were scored by two independent viewers with a medical background who were proficient in that language. Inter-rater agreement by Cohen's kappa, all p < 0.001: English 0.62, isiZulu 0.49, isiXhosa 0.82, Afrikaans 0.73, Nigerian Pidgin 1.00, Hausa 0.93, Twi 1.00, Arabic 0.82, French 0.44, Swahili 0.51, Amharic 1.00 (Table 1). Scoring criteria for the accompanying MICI components were developed from WHO and CDC guidelines; the misleading category itself is defined against scientific accuracy / evidence base. No adjudication procedure for disagreements is described.
estimates.moderator_quote: YouTube was accessed on 5 September 2020, using a new account with default settings, after clearing the cache of the Internet browser to minimize bias caused by cookies, personal preferences, and browser history. Combinations of search terms used included "coronavirus," and "COVID-19", and attaching the name of the language thereafter as a specifier [...] The first 50 relevant results were screened, and relevant videos that contained COVID-19 medical or epidemiological information were included.
estimates.notes: Rank-truncated search sample (first 50 relevant results per language per search term), hence denom_selection=curated; single-issue COVID-19 corpus, hence denom_scope=topical. Country is not reported at all - sampling is by language, not nation - so country_norm is Global rather than Multi-country. TWO FEATURES THAT PUSH THIS ESTIMATE DOWN and an adjudicator should note: (a) the content-type categories are mutually exclusive, so misleading claims inside 'personal experience' (n = 20) or 'news update' (n = 59) videos are not counted as misleading - the opposite of the convention used by e.g. Yeung et al., who reclassified personal-experience clips containing unsupported claims as misleading; (b) the denominator is the top search results, which in September 2020 were heavily weighted towards institutional and news content. The authors themselves attribute the low figure partly to the late timing relative to earlier studies.

estimates.country: Not specified; videos sampled by language across eleven languages widely spoken across Africa
estimates.measure_type: Mean reliability of COVID-19 YouTube videos on the modified DISCERN tool (0-5 scale; not a prevalence share)
estimates.value_raw: The mean total DISCERN score was 3.01 ± 1.11 out of a possible five
estimates.denominator: 562 YouTube videos containing COVID-19 medical or epidemiological information (same corpus as the CONTENT row)
estimates.definition: Modified DISCERN: five yes/no items (clarity of aims, reliable source, lack of bias, reference supplementation, mention of uncertainty), 1 point per 'yes', total 0 (lowest reliability) to 5 (highest)
estimates.misinfo_def: Not a misinformation definition: DISCERN scores reliability features of the video, not the truth of its claims
estimates.source_quote: The mean total DISCERN score was 3.01 ± 1.11 out of a possible five (Table 5 and Supplementary Table 2).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two language-proficient medical raters per language; kappa values as in the CONTENT row. DISCERN items adapted from prior YouTube studies.
estimates.moderator_quote: The reliability was evaluated using a modified DISCERN tool. This tool comprises five questions assessed: clarity, reliable source, lack of bias, reference supplementation, and mention of uncertainty; each has "Yes" or "No" responses.
estimates.notes: QUALITY row, kept for the record and excluded from prevalence: DISCERN is a reliability instrument, not a veracity judgement, and the result is a scale mean rather than a share of items. value_pct carries the score on its own 0-5 scale, NOT a percentage - do not read 3.01 as 3%.

estimates.country: Not specified; videos sampled by language across eleven languages widely spoken across Africa
estimates.measure_type: Mean quality of COVID-19 YouTube videos on the Medical Information Content Index (0-25 scale; not a prevalence share)
estimates.value_raw: The mean total MICI score was 5.75/25 (SD 4.35)
estimates.denominator: 562 YouTube videos containing COVID-19 medical or epidemiological information (same corpus as the CONTENT row)
estimates.definition: Medical Information Content Index: a 5-point Likert scale applied to each of five medical information components (prevalence, transmission, clinical symptoms, screening/testing, treatment/outcomes), maximum 25; component criteria adapted from WHO and CDC guidance
estimates.misinfo_def: Not a misinformation definition: MICI scores the coverage and quality of medical content, not the truth of claims
estimates.source_quote: Overall, information on the transmission of COVID-19 was most prevalent (477/562 videos, 84.9%), whilst content covering screening or testing was least reported with less than a third of videos containing such information (Table 4 and Supplementary Table 2). The mean total MICI score was 5.75/25 (SD 4.35).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two language-proficient medical raters per language; MICI component criteria developed from WHO and CDC guidelines (Supplementary Table 2).
estimates.moderator_quote: Quality was assessed using the Medical Information Content Index (MICI) scale. [...] The MICI is a 5-point Likert scale assessing five components of medical information: prevalence, transmission, clinical symptoms, screening/testing, and treatment/outcomes of disease. A maximum score of 25 was possible.
estimates.notes: QUALITY row, kept for the record and excluded from prevalence. value_pct carries the score on its own 0-25 scale, NOT a percentage. Note a discrepancy in the paper: the Abstract reads 'The mean total MICI score was 5.75/5 (SD 4.25)' while the Results and Table 4 give 5.75/25 (SD 4.35); the Results version is correct since the instrument's maximum is 25.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Per-language misleading shares were NOT entered as separate rows: language is not a country, platform or measure split, six of the eleven languages have a zero numerator, and the pooled figure is the paper's headline. Table 3 gives them in full: English 0/75 (0%), isiZulu 1/54 (2%), isiXhosa 0/49 (0%), Afrikaans 2/50 (4%), Nigerian Pidgin 3/53 (6%), Hausa 3/40 (6%), Twi 1/45 (2%), Arabic 0/50 (0%), French 2/46 (4%), Swahili 0/50 (0%), Amharic 0/50 (0%) - these sum correctly to 12. Note the running text is sloppier than the table: it says misleading videos were 'found in isiZulu (1/54, 2%), Afrikaans (2/50, 4%), Nigerian Pidgin, and Hausa (both 3/50, 6%)', omitting Twi and French and giving Nigerian Pidgin's and Hausa's denominators as 50 when they are 53 and 40. Trust Table 3. (2) The MICI component coverage shares (e.g. transmission 477/562, 84.9%; screening/testing 163/562, 29.0%; prevalence 249/562, 44.3%; clinical symptoms 352/562, 62.6%; treatment 246/562, 43.8%) are shares of videos CONTAINING a type of information, not shares of misinformation, so they are not prevalence estimates. (3) Source-type shares (independent users 246/562, 43.8%; government 84; news agency 118; academic 93; adverts 21) are authorship, not veracity. (4) Figures cited from other studies were not extracted (R8): Osman et al.'s systematic review (about 41% of health content inaccurate or 'not useful', 19% useful, 44%/11% of articles), 'over 25% of videos being misleading' from refs 18-20, Li et al. ('over a quarter'), and Khatri et al. ('10% and 8% of misleading videos'). (5) The per-content-type MICI and DISCERN breakdowns (e.g. misleading videos' mean MICI 4.5/25, DISCERN 2.0/5) are quality scores computed within a 12-video subgroup and are too small and too far from prevalence to be worth rows. (6) Engagement metrics (277,708,221 total views; misleading videos' like:dislike ratio 49.15) are not prevalence.

rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis. Frame: YouTube accessed once, on 5 September 2020, from a new account with default settings and cleared cache; searches combined 'coronavirus' and 'COVID-19' with each of eleven language names; the first 50 relevant results per search were screened (75 for English because of higher volume), excluding non-medical, wrong-language, silent and duplicate videos, giving 562 videos saved to a playlist with URLs captured. No response rate applies. Coding: two independent viewers with a medical background and proficiency in the relevant language scored each language's videos for content type (informative / misleading / personal / news update), source type, the modified DISCERN reliability tool (5 yes-no items) and the MICI quality scale (five 5-point components, max 25, criteria built from WHO and CDC guidance). Inter-rater reliability reported per language as Cohen's kappa, ranging 0.44 (French) and 0.49 (isiZulu) to 1.00 (Nigerian Pidgin, Twi, Amharic), all p < 0.001; no disagreement-resolution procedure is described, and no kappa is reported separately for the misleading classification. Analysis in R Studio, chi-square and ANOVA, alpha 0.05. Author-acknowledged limitations: only eleven of thousands of African languages; no qualitative or behavioural component. Data available from the corresponding author on request. A preprint version exists.
